name: Spatial Visualization
blurb: Picture the shapes moving, turning or joining up.
childIntro: The first pair shows something happening to a shape. Make the same thing happen to the third shape in your head.
howItWorks: Pearson describes this as recognizing how two or more designs would look if they were combined, which may involve rotations or overlapping. It is the only NNAT type that needs imagined movement rather than a static rule, so it does not appear until second grade.
parentTip: The distractor that catches most children is a mirror image where a rotation was needed. Turning a shape and flipping it look the same for symmetrical shapes but completely different for others. Cut a shape out of paper and let your child physically turn it, then physically flip it, so the difference becomes obvious.

questions.prompt: The first shape turns. Turn the third shape the same way.

figure.alt: A blue right triangle turns a quarter turn. A green trapezoid must turn the same way.

questions.explanation: The first shape turns one quarter turn clockwise. Do exactly the same to the trapezoid. Choice b turned the other way.
questions.strategy: Turn your head to check. If the shape looks right with your head tipped one way, that is the direction.

questions.prompt: Make the same change happen.

figure.alt: A yellow flag flips all the way over. A green house must do the same.

questions.explanation: The shape turns halfway round, so it ends up upside down. Choices b and d only turned a quarter of the way.
questions.strategy: Half a turn means upside down. A quarter turn means lying on its side.

questions.prompt: Make the same change to the last shape.

figure.alt: An empty blue chevron becomes a small green plus sign. Now do the same to an empty blue upside-down triangle.

questions.explanation: A small shape is added in the middle, and nothing else changes. The wrong answers add the wrong shape, or change the outer one.
questions.strategy: Ask exactly what was added, then check nothing else moved.
